pharm: Inhibits fibrinolysis by blocking the binding of plasminogen and plasmin to fibrin, thereby preventing clot breakdown and reducing bleeding caused by excessive fibrinolysis
quick: Acute bleeding: 4-5 g in the first hour, then 1 g/hour (or 1.25 g/h) for about 8 hours or until controlled; max 30 g/24 h
Oral may be taken with or without food
Use only if clearly needed; safety not established
Reduce dose in renal impairment - drug is renally excreted and accumulates
Use with caution in hepatic impairment
Bleeding/clinical response, signs of thrombosis, CK and muscle symptoms, renal function
summary: Epsilon aminocaproic acid (aminocaproic acid) is an antifibrinolytic lysine analogue used to treat or prevent excessive bleeding caused by systemic hyperfibrinolysis or urinary fibrinolysis. It works by competitively blocking the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen and plasmin, preventing their attachment to fibrin and thereby inhibiting clot breakdown. For acute bleeding the usual regimen is a loading dose of about 4-5 g (orally or by infusion) in the first hour, followed by approximately 1-1.25 g per hour until bleeding is controlled, with a maximum of about 30 g in 24 hours. Because it stabilises clots, its principal hazards are thrombosis and, when fibrinolysis is actually protective, intravascular clotting. It must NOT be used in active disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) without concurrent heparin, and it is contraindicated in upper urinary tract bleeding because clots may obstruct the ureters. Rapid IV administration can cause hypotension and arrhythmia, and prolonged use can cause myopathy with rhabdomyolysis.
indications: Treatment of excessive bleeding resulting from systemic hyperfibrinolysis (e.g. after surgery such as cardiac surgery, in some haematologic and malignant conditions, or after thrombolytic therapy)
Treatment of bleeding from urinary fibrinolysis (e.g. lower urinary tract bleeding), with appropriate precautions
Other uses include adjunct in selected bleeding disorders and mucosal bleeding (per labelling/clinical practice)

dosage.d: About 4-5 g in the first hour
dosage.t: Oral or by slow IV infusion (diluted)
dosage.n: Begin with a loading dose to achieve effective levels quickly

dosage.d: About 1 to 1.25 g per hour, continued for around 8 hours or until bleeding is controlled
dosage.t: Continuous IV infusion or repeated oral doses

dosage.d: Dilute and infuse slowly; do not give by rapid IV injection
dosage.n: Rapid injection can cause hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmia

dosage.d: Reduce dose because the drug is renally excreted and may accumulate
dosage.n: Monitor closely for accumulation and toxicity

admin: Confirm the bleeding is due to hyperfibrinolysis; do NOT use in active DIC unless heparin is also given
Do not use for upper urinary tract bleeding - clot retention can obstruct the ureters and cause renal failure
Dilute intravenous doses and infuse slowly; avoid rapid IV injection because of hypotension and arrhythmia
Reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for accumulation
Monitor for signs of thrombosis (limb pain/swelling, chest pain, breathlessness, neurological symptoms) during therapy
With prolonged use, monitor creatine kinase and watch for muscle pain/weakness (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis)
moa: Epsilon aminocaproic acid is a synthetic analogue of the amino acid lysine. It binds reversibly to the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and plasmin, the kringle domains through which these molecules normally attach to fibrin. By occupying these sites it prevents plasminogen activation on the fibrin surface and blocks plasmin from binding to and degrading fibrin, thereby inhibiting fibrinolysis and stabilising formed clots. This reduces bleeding in states of excessive fibrinolytic activity. The same clot-stabilising action is responsible for its risk of pathological thrombosis.

absolute: Active intravascular clotting / disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) without concomitant heparin
Evidence of an active thrombotic or thromboembolic process
Upper urinary tract bleeding (risk of obstructive clots and renal failure)
relative: Conditions predisposing to thrombosis (hypercoagulable states, recent thromboembolism)
Concomitant prothrombotic agents (e.g. clotting factor concentrates, prothrombin complex)
Haematuria of upper urinary tract origin
monitor: Signs and symptoms of thrombosis (venous, arterial, cerebral)
Creatine kinase and muscle symptoms with prolonged use
Renal function and blood pressure (especially during IV infusion)

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established. Aminocaproic acid should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit clearly justifies the potential risk, given the lack of adequate data and its prothrombotic potential.
lact: There are limited data on use during breastfeeding; it is not known whether it is excreted in human milk. Use with caution and only if clearly needed.
renal: Aminocaproic acid is largely excreted unchanged by the kidneys and can accumulate in renal impairment, increasing the risk of toxicity. Reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor closely. It must not be used for upper urinary tract bleeding because clots may obstruct the renal pelvis/ureters.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; monitor the patient's clinical and laboratory status.

major: Prothrombotic agents - clotting factor concentrates (e.g. factor IX complex / anti-inhibitor coagulant complex) - markedly increased risk of thrombosis when combined
Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives - additive hypercoagulability/thrombosis risk
moderate: Other antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid) - additive effect and thrombosis risk
Tissue plasminogen activators/thrombolytics - antagonistic effects (aminocaproic acid reverses fibrinolysis)
minor: May theoretically affect the action of anticoagulants by stabilising clots
interactions.food: Oral doses may be taken with or without food
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum potassium; prolonged use can elevate creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes; affects fibrinolysis-related laboratory tests

common: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal discomfort
serious: Thrombosis and thromboembolism (venous, arterial, including cerebral and coronary)
Myopathy with muscle weakness, myoglobinuria and rhabdomyolysis (with prolonged use)
Acute renal failure (including from obstructing urinary clots)
Hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmia with rapid IV injection
emergency: Acute thrombotic event (myocardial infarction, stroke, pulmonary embolism)
Severe hypotension or arrhythmia during IV administration

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of venous or arterial thrombosis
Creatine kinase and muscle symptoms during prolonged administration
Blood pressure and heart rate during intravenous infusion
counsel: This medicine helps stop or prevent serious bleeding by keeping blood clots from breaking down too quickly
Tell your doctor immediately about chest pain, breathlessness, leg pain or swelling, weakness or trouble speaking - these may be signs of a clot
Report muscle pain, weakness or dark/cola-coloured urine, especially if you take it for a long time
If given by drip, it must run in slowly; report dizziness or feeling faint during the infusion
Take oral doses as directed and complete the course your doctor prescribes
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially clotting-factor products or the contraceptive pill
pk: Antifibrinolytic effect develops rapidly after a loading dose
Oral peak plasma concentration at about 2 hours; effective levels achieved quickly with IV loading
Elimination half-life approximately 1-2 hours; mainly renally excreted unchanged
Short - effect declines as the drug is cleared, so continuous or repeated dosing is needed during active bleeding
Store at room temperature; dilute injection before use per label and protect from freezing
pearls: Main hazard is thrombosis - it stabilises clots, so it must NOT be used in active DIC unless heparin is also given, nor where an active thrombotic process exists
Contraindicated in upper urinary tract bleeding - clots can obstruct the ureters and cause renal failure
Give IV slowly and diluted - rapid injection causes hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmia
Prolonged use can cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis - monitor CK and muscle symptoms
Reduce the dose in renal impairment as it is renally cleared and accumulates
missed: During acute treatment, dosing is managed by the healthcare team and timing should not be altered by the patient. For oral maintenance, if a dose is missed take it as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double up.
overdose: Acute or chronic overdose may cause thrombosis, hypotension, muscle injury (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis) and renal impairment; acute toxicity has been reported uncommonly. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with discontinuation of the drug, monitoring for and treating thrombosis, supporting blood pressure and renal function, and managing rhabdomyolysis. Aminocaproic acid is removed by haemodialysis and may be removed by peritoneal dialysis.
